rv.q: Transferred from London’s West End by way of Cambridge, Mass., this twinkly two-hander delivers lavishly on the promise of a rom-com: laughter, escape and fantasy.

The show's minimalism extends to its set by Soutra Gilmour: two oversize piles of luggage on a turntable—conceptually clever even if it may trigger unpleasant memories of long, foot-tapping waits at airport carousels.
The guy takes a Costco sirloin and turns it into Peter Luger.
So while this show held me for Act One with its considerable charm, by Act Two, it was hitting turbulence.
When Two Strangers does do that, it does achieve something magical, and those moments make you see what a smaller-scale musical can do successfully without a huge budget or soapy showmanship.
As the icing on the cake, not only have they fallen in love with each other but we’ve fallen in love with them as well.
Ultimately, it’s a rare and beautiful story about two individuals who serve as unlikely catalysts for their respective self-discoveries.
Infectiously whimsical and sentimental, the show juxtaposes these qualities against a New York reality that has little time for either.
Most of all, I can think of no two people better equipped to carry this delightful musical than Sam Tutty and Christiani Pitts.
Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) is a sweet, original musical about finding love in the Big Apple.
Tutty and Pitts do just that and make Two Strangers a terrific feel-good addition to this theater season.

Tutty’s appealing looks, pure voice, comic instincts, and obvious acting skills, and somehow resemblance to a living Teletubby make him the huge plus for a vital Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) run.
This is a show so charming, so adorable, that you can easily overlook its flaws.
It's also one of the more entertaining, in part because it relies on solid writing rather than distracting gimmicks.
And Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) definitely works.

What I found most surprising about this modest, appealing two-person musical, whose title more or less sums up what happens, was the reaction to it on the night I attended – the ecstatic cheers at the start; the mobbed stage door afterwards.
Whatever, the cases look imposingly ugly, and act as a creative handcuffs on the show.
The trouble is, that's often an apt description of the show itself, too.
But I should've known from its twee little title that this would not be for me, and I was unfortunately correct.
As meet-cutes go, this one turns very problematic in Act 2, if not before.
It's also one of the best new musicals of the year.
In a season crowded with gaudy overindulgence, this small, sweet musical carries its multi-layered cake with surprising elegance.
Utterly charming and winsomely quirky, this show evokes laughter and joy in equal measures, while also contending with moments of substance and painful truth.
With only two main characters with endearing personalities and superb voices singing some wonderful songs, it is easily one of the nicest theatrical experiences I’ve had in a long time.
Two Strangers is occasionally thin in its ambitions but never less than endearing.
If you are looking for great structure and exhilarating drama, look elsewhere.

This is a charming little show (which definitely doesn’t need to be two hours and twenty minutes long) that reminded me of another modest musical focusing on a mismatched pair — last year’s Maybe Happy Ending.
In fairness, the book offers plenty of laughs, thanks in large part to endearing performances by Tutty and Pitts.
Two Strangers is a near-perfect rom-com musical: witty and clever, yet reflective, gently nudging audiences to think about what family really means to them.
Happily, the charming new Broadway musical Two Strangers (Carry a Cake Across New York) gets things right.
Warm, witty, and easy to enjoy.

tn.cat: Best Scenic Design of a Musical

cn.t: This charming British rom-com musical wins hearts with its modest two-hander approach and winning leads, though some find the lightweight material and forgettable score more crumbs than confection.

lo.t: Opens 12 AM ET day before, closes with drawings at 10 AM and 3 PM ET
lo.inst: Enter at rush.telecharge.com. One entry per person per day. Limit 2 tickets per entry. Winners notified by email with limited window to purchase.

ru.t: 10 AM on the day of each performance
ru.loc: Longacre Theatre box office (220 W 48th St)
ru.inst: In person, first-come first-served. Limit 2 tickets per person.

sg.ra: Choose Rows D-L for a comfortable distance that retains stage detail. Center seats have a direct angle to the stage. Rows H-L are under the Mezzanine overhang, which can cut off the top of the stage.

Choose Rows A-C for excellent elevated views, with a clear view of the full performance from a comfortable distance. Expect to pay the highest prices in the Center Mezzanine for these front rows. Prefer Row A if avoiding the Balcony overhang matters, because it starts at Row B.
Rows D-E provide a clean, direct view of the stage. Expect a possible minor obstruction at the top of the stage because the Balcony overhang begins at Row B.

Choose rows A or B in the Center Balcony for the best overhead views in this section. They give a clear, complete view but are distant, so fine details are less clear. These seats are especially effective for musicals with ensemble choreography.

Avoid the last few Balcony rows if you can because the view is not great and sound issues have been reported. Seats behind the pillars between rows B and C can have bisected sightlines, although you may be able to lean around them. If you must sit here, choose an aisle seat for more legroom.

sn.c: The Mezzanine overhang kicks in at row H, and seats behind this may experience cut-off at the top of the stage.
sn.sh: Mezzanine overhang kicks in at row H

sn.lo: Center Orchestra, rows AA to B
sn.c: Rows AA, A and B can be too close because the angle leads to neck craning.
sn.sh: Rows AA to B can be too close

sn.c: Towards the far sides in the Left and Right Mezzanine, views tend to become more obstructed by the Boxes and the angle towards the stage.
sn.sh: Far side views tend to be more obstructed

sn.lo: Center Balcony, rows B to C
sn.c: Four thin pillars are located between rows B and C at the edge of the Center Balcony.
sn.sh: Thin pillars between rows B and C

sn.c: The middle rows in the Center Mezzanine are a good value option for elevated sightlines that don’t feel distant.
sn.sh: Elevated sightlines that don’t feel distant

sn.lo: Center Balcony, rows A to B
sn.c: Rows A and B of the Center Balcony are the best views in this high and more distant section.
sn.sh: Best views in the Balcony section

vs.sum: The Longacre Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions, even from the balcony, and the sound quality is consistently praised. While the seating is a bit narrow, it provides average comfort for most patrons. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant Beaux Arts interior, and facilities are typical for a Broadway venue, with some lines at intermission but generally manageable.

acc.note: Small restroom-only elevator (may not accommodate all wheelchairs). 3 wheelchair spaces in Orchestra.

Two Strangers is easily the early frontrunner for next year's Best Musical. It's a real charmer that has all the makings of a hit — good music, lovely performances, emotional substance, and maybe most charming of all, it's unexpected.
I recommend this thoroughly to just about anyone who loves New York theater... I love the show.
I cannot recommend this one enough
